slides.title: Money questions you're scared to ask

slides.q: What does APY mean on a savings account?
slides.a: APY stands for annual percentage yield. It's how much your money earns in a year, including interest on your interest. So $1,000 at 4% APY would earn about $40 in a year if the rate stays the same. Savings rates can change anytime, so compare banks and check that your account is FDIC insured.

slides.q: Should I ask for a credit limit increase?
slides.a: It can help your credit score, because using a smaller share of your limit looks better to lenders. Some card issuers do a hard credit check when you ask, which can dip your score a little, so ask them first. The real rule: only do it if a higher limit won't tempt you to spend more.

slides.q: Is it bad to pay rent with a credit card?
slides.a: Not always, but watch the fees. Many landlords and payment sites charge around 3% for cards, which usually wipes out any rewards you'd earn. If there's no fee and you pay the full balance every month, it's fine. Carrying rent on a card and paying interest is where it gets expensive fast.

slides.q: What happens if I just don't file my taxes?
slides.a: If you owe money, the IRS adds a penalty of 5% of the unpaid tax for each month you're late, up to 25%, plus interest. If you're owed a refund, there's no penalty, but you only get about three years to claim it. Missed it? File as soon as you can. It usually only gets worse.

slides.q: What's a grace period on a credit card?
slides.a: It's the time between when your statement closes and when your payment is due, usually at least 21 days. If you pay the full statement balance by the due date, you don't pay interest on new purchases. Pay only part of it and you can lose the grace period, so interest starts adding up right away.
